Q: Why Java Byte[] to Int/Int to Byte[] need operation "&0xFF" A:

In Java, byte is a signed integral type. That means it can represent negative numbers as well as positive. It's why the value range of byte is [-128, 127] instead of [0, 255]. And the way Java represents signed integral types is with two's complement.

For example, if you have byte b = -2; then the binary representation of b would be:

11111110

Doing b & 0xFF then does two things:

  1. It first promotes b to an int. This is a widening conversion, which for signed integral types involves sign extension.
  2. It performs the bitwise AND operation on the two operands: (int) b and 0xFF. Note that 0xFF is an int and is the hexadecimal representation of 255 (in decimal).

In binary, that would look like:

  11111111 11111111 11111111 11111110
& 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111
―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――
  00000000 00000000 00000000 11111110

The result in decimal is 254 and is the unsigned value of b. In other words, doing b & 0xFF for a given byte b will give you the unsigned value of b as an int.

When converting a byte[4] into an int you need to use the unsigned byte values because you don't want the leading 1 bits of a negative number when bit shifting. Let's say you have 42,117 in a byte array:

// 42,117
byte[] b = {0, 0, -92, -63};

You would convert that array into an int like so:

int b0 = (b[0] & 0xFF) << 24;
int b1 = (b[1] & 0xFF) << 16;
int b2 = (b[2] & 0xFF) <<  8;
int b3 = (b[3] & 0xFF);
int i  = b0 | b1 | b2 | b3; // 42,177

Which in binary would look like:

  (00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111) << 24
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111) << 16
| (11111111 11111111 11111111 10100100 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111) <<  8
| (11111111 11111111 11111111 11000001 & 00000000 00000000 00000000 11111111)

=>

  (00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000) << 24
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000) << 16
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 10100100) <<  8
| (00000000 00000000 00000000 11000001)

=>

  00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000
| 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000
| 00000000 00000000 10100100 00000000
| 00000000 00000000 00000000 11000001
―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――
  00000000 00000000 10100100 11000001

The result is the binary representation of 42,177, which is the correct value.

If you didn't include the & 0xFF then the leading 1 bits of the negative bytes would remain, and you'd ultimately end up with (after shifting):

  00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000
| 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000
| 11111111 11111111 10100100 00000000
| 11111111 11111111 11111111 11000001
―――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――――
  11111111 11111111 11111111 11000001

The result is now the binary representation of -63, which is the incorrect value.

The same reasoning applies when going from an int to a byte[4]. However, you can use the >>> operator instead and avoid the & 0xFF, at least for the first 3 bytes. That operator does not extend the sign like the >> operator does.

public static byte[] toBytes(int i) {
  byte[] b = new byte[4];
  b[0] = (byte) (i >>> 24);
  b[1] = (byte) (i >>> 16);
  b[2] = (byte) (i >>>  8);
  b[3] = (byte) (i & 0xFF);
  return b;
}

Q: Using R to count instances of strings where the order of the letters isn't important A:

For each string, sort its characters, put them back together and count the frequencies with table.

fun <- function(x) {
  lapply(x, strsplit, "") |> 
    unlist(recursive = FALSE) |>
    lapply(sort) |> 
    sapply(paste, collapse = "") |>
    table(useNA = "ifany")
}

fun(offspring)
#> 
#> aabb aabB aaBB aAbb aAbB aABB AAbb AAbB AABB 
#>    1    2    1    2    4    2    1    2    1

Created on 2026-03-03 with reprex v2.1.1

You can output as a data.frame by piping the above to as.data.frame.

fun(offspring) |> as.data.frame()
#>   Var1 Freq
#> 1 aabb    1
#> 2 aabB    2
#> 3 aaBB    1
#> 4 aAbb    2
#> 5 aAbB    4
#> 6 aABB    2
#> 7 AAbb    1
#> 8 AAbB    2
#> 9 AABB    1
